newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl criticised for shunning Russia's Lebed.
newsitem.headline: Kohl criticised for shunning Russia's Lebed.

text.p: General Alexander Lebed may not be Germany's idea of the perfect Russian president but he is a potential leader whom Chancellor Helmut Kohl should not have shunned, commentators and politicians said on Thursday.

On the third day of a trip intended to introduce himself to Germany as a potential successor to the ailing Boris Yeltsin, Lebed met party leaders and foreign policy experts, and was due to address his second gathering of industrialists.

Lebed, easily Russia's most popular politician, has been welcomed warmly, but ignored by the government and by Kohl, a staunch supporter of Yeltsin who declined to waive protocol to receive a man with no political office.

The remaining establishment has found plenty to criticise in Lebed's comments. It has also found a formidable politician in the ex-paratroop general who came a strong third in last year's Russian election but has almost no foreign political experience.
"We can't choose the people who have leading positions in Russia, but we have to deal with them," said Karsten Voigt, foreign policy spokesman of the opposition Social Democrats.
Bonn's General-Anzeiger daily said Lebed had been too keen to use his trip to score points at home, but that Yeltsin's frailty was inescapable.
"For that reason Bonn must find a more relaxed attitude to dealing with (Yeltsin's) democratic rivals," it said.

The Mannheimer Morgen went further: "Helmut Kohl has no desire to receive the former security adviser of his pal Boris. The chancellor doesn't want to accept the fact that the Yeltsin era is slowly ending."
It contrasted what it saw as Kohl's exaggerated loyalty with the attitude of U.S. President Bill Clinton, who has invited Lebed to his forthcoming inauguration in Washington.
Lebed has failed to convince commentators that he has an effective remedy to Russia's economic and social crisis, but has given the impression that he takes Western and German concerns seriously.

He earned few plaudits for setting out a vision of economic revival based on state control of consumer goods and a state monopoly of foreign trade, as well as scepticism towards the remedies of the International Monetary Fund.

Voigt told Southwest German Radio that Lebed had ideas "which he probably thinks are to do with a market economy but in fact are really about a new leadership steering the whole thing in a more honest direction".
"Those are words that certainly sound good but don't contain much in the way of a big idea."

He said Lebed's vision of democracy was a particularly authoritarian one, but praised him for at least showing flexibility in defending Russia's opposition to an eastward enlargement of the Western NATO alliance.

"He is a man who doesn't want confrontation with western Europe, the West or NATO. But he is also a man who I hope will still learn a lot about European realities. Because the way he talked to us, apparently thinking he was coming across very well...left a lot of question marks."
